title: Science: Pushes, Pulls, and Changes
objectives: I can use ten science words to explain how forces and energy change motion.
I can tell what friction, gravity, and other words mean from a science journal.
I can use the endings -ion, -ance, and -er to understand science words.
I can write a short science explanation using exact verbs.
rationale: Grade 4 science asks students to explain how forces and energy change what things do. Three named physical-science terms (friction, gravity, vibrate) are paired with Tier 2 verbs (deflect, reflect, ignite, compress, resist, release, propel) that students need in order to describe cause and effect in a lab report. Two of the verbs (reflect, release) have other meanings, so the unit fixes the science sense first. The passage is a camping journal, so students meet the words in familiar events rather than in textbook definitions. These words come back in every later science unit on energy, light, and sound.

words.def: A force that slows things when two surfaces rub together.
words.ex: Friction between the tires and the road helps a car stop.
words.ex2: Rubbing your hands together makes them warm because of friction.
words.nonExample: Two surfaces that never touch cannot make friction.

apps.academic: In science, friction turns some of an object's motion into heat.
apps.spoken: There's less friction on the ice, so I slide farther.
apps.writing: Use friction to explain why a moving object slows down.

cloze.s: Sandpaper creates a lot of ___ when you rub it on wood, so the wood heats up and wears away.

cloze2.s: A thin layer of oil reduces ___ between the metal gears so they turn smoothly.

misuse.s: Friction makes a sliding box speed up as it rubs against the floor.
misuse.why: Friction slows moving things down; it does not speed them up.

visual.alt: Two hands rubbing together with a small flame for heat.

words.def: The force that pulls objects toward the center of Earth.
words.ex: Gravity pulled the apple from the tree to the grass.
words.ex2: On the Moon, gravity is weaker than on Earth, so astronauts can jump higher.
words.nonExample: A magnet picking up a paper clip shows magnetism, not gravity.

apps.academic: In science, gravity explains why planets stay in orbit around the sun.
apps.spoken: Gravity pulls everything down to the ground.
apps.writing: Use gravity to explain why dropped objects fall.

cloze.s: When Leo let go of the ball, ___ pulled it down to the floor.

cloze2.s: Because the Moon's ___ is weaker than Earth's, an astronaut can jump much higher there.

misuse.s: Gravity pushes a dropped ball upward toward the ceiling.
misuse.why: Gravity pulls things down toward Earth; it does not push them up.

visual.alt: An apple falling downward from a tree.

words.def: To shake back and forth very quickly.
words.ex: The guitar string vibrates when you pluck it.
words.ex2: My phone vibrated on the table when a message came in.
words.nonExample: A rock sitting still does not vibrate.

apps.academic: Sound is made when something vibrates and sends waves through the air.
apps.spoken: My throat vibrates when I hum.
apps.writing: Use vibrate for fast back-and-forth movement, such as a string or a speaker.

cloze.s: Touch your throat while humming, and you can feel your voice box ___.

cloze2.s: The tuning fork began to ___ and made a clear, ringing sound.

misuse.s: The drum stayed perfectly still as it vibrated and made a loud sound.
misuse.why: To vibrate is to shake quickly; a drum making sound must be shaking.

visual.alt: A guitar with wavy lines showing the strings shaking.

words.def: To make something bounce off or turn aside.
words.ex: The goalie dove and deflected the shot with her fingertips.
words.ex2: A sloped roof can deflect rain away from the windows.
words.nonExample: A ball that rolls straight through an open gate has not been deflected.

apps.academic: A shield can deflect an object by changing its direction.
apps.spoken: The wall deflected the ball back to me.
apps.writing: Use deflect for a push that changes the direction of something moving.

cloze.s: The shield was built to ___ the arrows so they bounced away from the knight.

cloze2.s: Hold the umbrella at an angle to ___ the rain away from your backpack.

misuse.s: The goalie deflected the shot by catching the ball and holding it still.
misuse.why: To deflect is to turn something aside; catching and holding it does not change its direction.

visual.alt: A goalie's glove turning a ball aside near the net.

words.def: To send light, heat, or sound back from a surface.
words.ex: A mirror will reflect your face.
words.ex2: Snow can reflect so much sunlight that it hurts your eyes.
words.nonExample: A thick black cloth that soaks up light does not reflect it well.

apps.academic: A smooth, shiny surface will reflect most of the light that hits it.
apps.writing: Use reflect for light or sound that bounces off a surface.

cloze.s: The calm lake can ___ the mountains so well that it looks like a second sky.

cloze2.s: White clothes ___ sunlight, so they feel cooler than dark clothes on a hot day.

misuse.s: The mirror reflects nothing, so you cannot see yourself in it at all.
misuse.why: A mirror reflects light and shows your image.

visual.alt: A mirror catching sunlight and sending it back.

words.def: To start burning or to make something start burning.
words.ex: A single spark can ignite dry leaves.
words.ex2: The engine starts when the spark plug ignites the fuel.
words.nonExample: A candle that has been blown out is not ignited.

apps.academic: A fire needs heat, fuel, and oxygen to ignite and keep burning.
apps.spoken: Be careful; a spark can ignite dry grass.
apps.writing: Use ignite for the moment something begins to burn.

cloze.s: Dad struck the match to ___ the dry kindling, and the sticks began to burn.

cloze2.s: Never let sparks drift near dry grass, because they can ___ a wildfire.

misuse.s: Pouring water on the logs will ignite them and start the campfire.
misuse.why: Water puts out fires; it does not start them.

visual.alt: A flame starting on a stack of logs.

words.def: To press something so it takes up less space.
words.ex: She had to compress her sleeping bag to fit it into the sack.
words.ex2: A bicycle pump compresses air into a tire.
words.nonExample: Stretching a spring makes it longer; it does not compress it.

apps.academic: Gases are easy to compress because their particles are far apart.
apps.spoken: Compress the foam, and watch it spring back.
apps.writing: Use compress for squeezing something into a smaller space.

cloze.s: Press down hard to ___ the foam, and you will see it shrink to half its size.

cloze2.s: Before packing, she tried to ___ her sweaters into a flat bundle.

misuse.s: Compress the balloon by letting it fill up and grow bigger.
misuse.why: To compress is to squeeze into less space; growing bigger is the opposite.

visual.alt: A box being squeezed flat by a downward arrow.

words.def: To push back against a force or refuse to give in.
words.ex: Strong walls resist the wind during a storm.
words.ex2: It is hard to resist a warm cookie that smells that good.
words.nonExample: A leaf that is blown away by the wind does not resist it.

apps.academic: Some materials resist heat better than others, which is why pot handles are made of plastic.
apps.writing: Use resist for holding up against a push or a temptation.

cloze.s: A thick wool coat helps you ___ the cold wind that blows across the open field.

cloze2.s: The little boat could not ___ the strong current and drifted downstream.

misuse.s: The glass resisted the hammer by shattering into a hundred pieces.
misuse.why: To resist is to hold up against a force; shattering is the opposite.

visual.alt: A brick wall standing firm against strong wind.

words.def: To let go of something so it is free to move.
words.ex: When you release the string, the kite flies up.
words.ex2: The scientist will release the ball from the top of the ramp.
words.nonExample: Holding on tightly to a rope is not releasing it.

apps.academic: In an experiment, you release a toy car at the top of a ramp and time how far it rolls.
apps.spoken: Release the button and the toy will stop.
apps.writing: Use release for the moment you let something go.

cloze.s: When Nia opened her hand to ___ the ball, it dropped straight to the floor.

cloze2.s: A stretched rubber band shoots across the room the moment you ___ it.

misuse.s: She released the bird by locking it inside a small cage.
misuse.why: To release is to let go and set free; locking it in a cage is the opposite.

visual.alt: Open hands letting a bird fly away.

words.ex: Strong legs propel a swimmer through the water.
words.ex2: The engine propels the boat across the bay.
words.nonExample: A boat that sits at the dock is not being propelled.

apps.academic: A rocket engine propels a rocket upward by pushing hot gas out of its base.
apps.spoken: She used her arms to propel the canoe.
apps.writing: Use propel for a push that sends something forward.

cloze.s: Four strong oars can ___ the rowboat across the pond, even against a light wind.

cloze2.s: A burst of air from the balloon will ___ the toy car along the table.

misuse.s: The engine propels the boat by pulling it backward toward the dock.
misuse.why: To propel is to push forward; pulling backward is the opposite.

visual.alt: A person rowing a boat forward over the water.

passage.title: Nia's Science Journal: Camping Weekend
paras: Saturday. Dad showed me how to ignite a campfire. He rubbed the match head against the side of the box. The friction made heat, and the match burst into flame. We touched it to dry grass, and soon the sticks were burning.
At sunset, I had to compress my sleeping bag to fit it into a small sack. When I released the strap, the bag puffed back up like a balloon.

Sunday. We paddled a canoe across the lake. Each pull of the paddle propelled us forward. The wind tried to resist us by pushing against the canoe, so we had to paddle harder. The water was so calm that it could reflect the pine trees like a mirror.

On the hike back, a loose rock rolled down the slope because of gravity. It hit a tree trunk, and the trunk deflected it to the side. Later, thunder rumbled so loudly that I could feel it vibrate in my chest. I wrote one sentence in my journal: forces are everywhere, even at a campsite.

qs.q: In paragraph 1, the word "ignite" most nearly means
qs.why: The match bursts into flame and soon the sticks are burning.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the wind tries to "resist" the canoe. What does the wind do?
qs.why: The wind pushes against the canoe, so Nia has to paddle harder.

qs.q: Why did the match burst into flame?
choices: The sun was shining on it.
Rubbing the match on the box made heat.
qs.why: Friction made heat, which started the flame.

qs.q: Which sentence best shows the effect of gravity?
choices: Each pull of the paddle propelled us forward.
The water was so calm that it could reflect the pine trees.
Dad showed me how to ignite a campfire.
A loose rock rolled down the slope because of gravity.
qs.why: The rock rolls down the slope because gravity pulls it down.

qs.q: What is the main idea of Nia's journal?
choices: Canoes are the best way to travel.
Forces and energy can be seen in everyday events, even on a camping trip.
qs.why: Each entry describes a force at work, and the last line sums it up.

write.prompt: Describe a force you saw at work today, such as a push, a pull, or something sliding. Use at least three science words from this unit.
write.frame: I saw ___ when ___. This happened because ___.

study.task: Choose a verb from the unit and add -ion, -ance, or -er to make a noun. Tell what the new noun means and use it in a science sentence.

shades.label: how tightly something is pushed together

Write a sentence about an object that vibrates. Say what you can feel or hear.
Write a sentence that uses gravity and fall.

constructed.prompt: A toy car rolls down a ramp and then slows on the floor. Explain what happens using friction and gravity.

ties each force to the ramp or floor

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that describe forces, motion, and change, read a camping journal in which each word shows up in real events, practice the suffixes -ion, -ance, and -er, and write short science explanations.

notes.va.friction.n: Have students rub their hands together and describe the heat. Contrast friction with air resistance; both slow motion, but friction needs two surfaces.
notes.va.gravity.n: Gravity pulls toward the center of Earth. Students may say gravity only works on falling objects; remind them it works on everything.
notes.va.vibrate.v: Use a ruler over a desk edge or a tuning fork. Link vibrate to sound and to the passage's thunder.
notes.va.deflect.v: Deflect changes direction. Contrast with reflect, which sends light, heat, or sound back, and with stop, which ends motion.
notes.va.reflect.v: Teach the science sense first (light or sound bouncing off a surface). The thinking sense, as in reflecting on a book, is a different meaning.
notes.va.ignite.v: Keep fire safety in front of students: adults ignite fires. Use pictures of a campfire or an engine.
notes.va.compress.v: Use a sponge or a foam ball to feel compress and expand. Compare compress to squeeze.
notes.va.resist.v: Resist means push back or hold up against. It appears with temptation too; point out that sense briefly.
notes.va.release.v: Teach the verb sense: let go and set free. Use a ball and a rubber band. The noun release, as in a new game, is a different use.
notes.va.propel.v: Propel means push forward. Pair with propeller to show the family. Ask what propels a bicycle, a canoe, a rocket.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The rock rolls down the slope. I need a word for the force that pulls it down. That is gravity. The text says because of gravity, so I can write: Gravity pulled the rock down the hill.'
discuss: Which of these words describe things that start motion? Which describe things that slow or turn motion?
How can you tell the difference between reflect and deflect in a sentence?
misconceptions: Friction always makes things warm only; it also wears things down.
Gravity only pulls things on Earth.
To reflect always means to think.
Vibrate means to move in a straight line.
extend: Design a short experiment on friction using a ramp and different surfaces; write results using five words from the unit.
Write a 'How it works' paragraph for a spring toy using compress, release, and propel.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit friction, gravity, and resist as a force trio two days later, again at one week, and reuse projectile, terrain, and because of when students explain motion.

wida.oral: Partner A makes a motion (pressing, letting go, pushing). Partner B names the word from this unit and says the force at work.

needsReview: Science facts (friction makes heat, a match head ignites by rubbing, gravity pulls toward Earth's center, Moon gravity is weaker, thunder can be felt as a vibration) are standard; confirm against the classroom science text.
Spanish glosses (desviar, soltar, impulsar, encender) not reviewed by a native speaker; encender for ignite is the common everyday choice.
Reflect and release have other senses (to think about; a new product); only the science sense is taught here.
